question.text: Mr. Vikram Rao runs a family office with INR 200 crore. He wants (a) daily liquidity on 60% of the corpus, (b) discretionary customised equity management on 25%, and (c) exposure to unlisted late-stage growth companies on 15%. Per NISM Ch 2.4, which combination of investment channels is MOST appropriate?

answer.text: (a) Fixed Deposit, (b) Mutual Fund, (c) Stock Broker
(a) Category III AIF, (b) Mutual Fund, (c) Specialized Investment Fund
(a) Mutual Fund / ETF, (b) Portfolio Management Services, (c) Category II AIF (PE Fund)

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 2.4: (a) Daily liquidity and diversified listed exposure = open-ended Mutual Fund or ETF (Ch 2.4.2.1). (b) Discretionary customised management for HNIs = PMS (Ch 2.4.2.2). (c) Unlisted late-stage growth = Cat II AIF Private Equity fund (Ch 2.4.2.3 + Ch 2.3.2). This aligns each objective with the channel whose regulatory and structural design fits it. The Trap: Option A over-uses AIF for a need (daily liquidity) that AIF structurally cannot provide. Option C uses FD (not managed portfolio) and mis-tags a stock broker as a channel for unlisted investing. Option D mis-places Cat III AIF (hedge strategy) for daily liquidity, and mis-uses SIF for unlisted late-stage. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-A (PMS Distributor) and XIX-A (Cat I/II Distributor) test this matching from distribution side. XIX-C tests it as a manager-of-managers allocation decision. Manager's Pro-Tip: Help your family-office LPs map objective-to-vehicle in writing. A one-page allocation framework (liquidity bucket = MF, customised = PMS, illiquid growth = AIF, sophisticated MF = SIF) prevents the common mistake of stuffing everything into AIF and then hitting lockup crises.
